title: Scope and lifetime
goal: Distinguish name scope from object lifetime and predict independent calls.

prerequisites.text: Understand blocks, numeric functions and an accumulator.

terms.title: Scope
terms.definition: The region of source text where a name refers to a declaration.

terms.title: Lifetime
terms.definition: The period of execution during which the object exists.

sections.title: Why it matters
paragraphs: Every trip needs its own total. If it survives between calls, the next calculation accidentally inherits an earlier result.
Scope concerns the source, while lifetime concerns execution. Local static retains a value across calls without widening name visibility.
On a function declaration, static gives the name internal linkage: it can name this function within the source file. Local static on minutes gives the object a lifetime that spans the entire program.
Scope tells you where you can name a variable. Lifetime tells you when its value is stored. Separate trips test whether the accumulator carries over between calls.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Find the two step variables. Explain which one is used inside the inner block and which one is printed.
steps: Inner block → step 2 → total 10 → Inner object
After block → new step 7 → 10 7 → Different object

sections.title: Diagnostics
paragraphs: Find the block boundary when the compiler reports an undeclared name. The inner step is outside its scope after the closing brace.
Two calls with equal arguments expose unwanted accumulation in a local static.

sections.title: Transfer to practice
paragraphs: Equal trips should take equal time. An ordinary local accumulator starts at zero on each call. A returned number can be stored after the function exits.

Draw the name's boundaries separately from the execution timeline. In both versions the name minutes is local. In the trace, the second call either gets a new object initialized to zero or updates the same object again. The difference is lifetime, regardless of the spelling of the name.

selfcheck.prompt: Why might the starter print 6 12 for equal trips?
Why do two repaired calls give 6 6 for 2 and 2?
selfcheck.feedback: Each call owns a minutes initialised to zero. Two additions of 3 produce 6 independently of the prior call.

practice.title: Independent trips
practice.task: Enter two trips with 0 to 10 stops each. Each stop adds 3 minutes to its trip. Repair trip_minutes so calls do not share a total. Print two results or invalid. The supplied read_integer function checks the first two lines. A missing line, an invalid number or an out-of-range value gives invalid. The program ignores any later input.
practice.hint: Trace the initial minutes on each call.
criteria: A call is independent of the previous call.

steps.action: Enter 2 on each of two lines, then run the starter.
steps.why: Distinguish name scope from object lifetime and predict independent calls.
steps.expected: The starter prints 6 12. Two identical trips should give 6 6.

steps.action: Trace the starting value of minutes for each call. Fix the accumulator and try 2 and 2, then 10 and 0.
steps.why: The change must satisfy the contract.
steps.expected: The corrected output is 6 6 for two trips with two stops each, and 30 0 for ten and zero stops.

steps.action: Check a distinct boundary case and explain the result.
steps.why: Different cases distinguish the parts of the rule.
steps.expected: A call is independent of the previous call.

exercises.title: Independent transfer
exercises.task: Show the starting and ending totals for trips of 2 and 4 stops before and after the fix.
criteria: Before the fix the second call goes from 6 to 18.
After the fix it goes from 0 to 12.

teaching.scene: A route needs a temporary adjustment on its first segment. The overall total survives the segment, while the temporary name can be declared again. Check which variable is visible at each point.

predict.prompt: total starts at 8. The inner block declares step = 2, and code after it declares step = 7. Which two values are available to printf?
predict.answer: The inner step adds 2 to total and goes out of scope at the closing brace. The later step is 7. The printed pair is 10 7.

apply.prompt: Compare two trips with 3 and 1 stops in the same run. What happens with an ordinary local minutes and with minutes retained between calls? Name the observation that distinguishes the two versions.
apply.answer: With an ordinary local accumulator each call starts at 0, so the output is 9 3. If the accumulator incorrectly persists, the second call starts at 9 and the output is 9 12. The first number matches, so check the second.

practice.strategy: Decide which data belongs to one call of trip_minutes. Trace the starting value of each sum and try two identical routes in the same run.
practice.diagnosis: If two routes of two stops give 6 12, the second calculation likely inherited the first total. Inspect the lifetime of the variable that holds the minutes.

syntax.explanation: The inner declaration is visible from its declaration through the end of the block. An outer variable can keep a value assigned by that block.
syntax.mistake: A local `static` name retains its block scope, and its stored value persists between calls. Independent calculations depend on both properties.
